title: Maqqef, the accents and reading a verse

objectives.can: Read words joined by maqqef as one unit, recognise sof pasuq, atnah and silluq, and read a whole verse aloud.

explanation.summary: Besides vowel points, a printed Hebrew Bible carries a second set of signs, the accents, and a short stroke called maqqef that joins two words. They mark the stress, show how a verse divides into parts, and served as notation for chanting. Learning a few of them lets you read a whole verse as the tradition does.

sections.heading: Maqqef: two words as one
body: A maqqef is a short horizontal stroke written at the top of the line between two words. It joins them, so that they are read as a single unit with a single stress, on the last word. The first word loses its own stress and its vowel is often shortened.

In the second verse of Genesis the word עַל, 'upon', is joined to the word פְּנֵי, 'the face of', and the two are read as one: 'al-pe-NE'. Small words such as עַל, אֶת (the mark of the definite object), כִּי, 'that', and אֶל, 'to', are very often joined in this way to the word that follows. In this edition the maqqef is printed at the end of the first word, followed by a space.

sections.heading: The accents
body: The accents are small signs written above or below a word, usually beside the stressed syllable. They do three jobs. They mark the stress. They divide the verse, a little like punctuation, showing which words belong closely together. And they served as a notation for chanting the text in synagogue reading; the melodies differ among communities, and this lesson does not teach them.

There are two kinds. A disjunctive accent separates a word from the next, like a comma or a full stop. A conjunctive accent joins a word to the next. Many words carry a conjunctive accent; the disjunctives are fewer, and they carry the structure of the verse.

sections.heading: Three signs to know
body: The sof pasuq ('end of the verse') is a pair of dots, one above the other, written after the last word of every verse. It is followed by the next verse. Just before it, on the last word, stands a short vertical stroke under the stressed syllable: the silluq. The silluq and the sof pasuq always come together at the end of a verse.

The atnah is a small sign like an arrowhead under the stressed syllable of one word. It marks the main division in the middle of the verse and splits it into two halves. The words after the atnah are read as the second half. A very short verse may have no atnah, since it needs no division.

Other disjunctive accents divide each half further. The most common is the zaqef, a small sign above a word, which marks a smaller pause inside a half of the verse. Others, with names such as tifcha, revia and tevir, divide the parts again. Grammarians describe the system as a ranking, with the sof pasuq and the atnah at the top, and the smaller dividers below. You do not need to learn them all to read; recognise the three main signs and notice the others as pauses.

sections.heading: Reading a verse aloud
body: Take the verse in steps. First find the end, the sof pasuq with the silluq on the last word. Then find the atnah: that is the end of the first half. Then look for any maqqef, and group the words it joins. For each word find the syllables and the stress, and read the vowels as the points show them: a short vowel in a closed syllable, a long one in an open or stressed syllable.

Now read the verse in two parts, pausing slightly at the atnah and at the other disjunctive accents, and stopping at the end. Genesis 1:1 divides at the atnah after אֱלֹהִים, 'God': the first half is 'In the beginning God created' and the second half names what he created.

sections.heading: Ketiv and qere
body: In a number of places the consonants of the written text (the ketiv, 'what is written') differ from the word the tradition reads (the qere, 'what is read'). The reading tradition did not change the consonants; it marked the word to be read instead. The edition behind these lessons prints the word the tradition reads.

misunderstandings: An accent sign is not a vowel point. The vowel stays; the accent is a second mark beside it.
The silluq looks like the stroke of the meteg, a small sign that marks a secondary stress. The silluq is only the one on the last word, just before the sof pasuq.
Words joined by a maqqef are not two stresses. They are one unit with one stress.
Not every verse has an atnah. A very short verse may be undivided.
The sof pasuq is not a full stop in the English sense. It is the sign that ends a verse, and a verse can contain more than one sentence or less than a sentence.

deeper.heading: Two systems of accents
body: The accents described here belong to the twenty-one books of the Bible that are usually called the prose books. The three poetic books, Psalms, Proverbs and Job, have a different system, with some of the same signs used in other ways. This course meets that system only when it reaches poetry.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The atnah stands on אֱלֹהִים and divides the verse: 'In the beginning God created' is the first half, and 'the heavens and the earth' is the second. The last word, הָאָרֶץ, carries the silluq under its stressed syllable, and the sof pasuq follows it. The other words carry the smaller divider tifcha or conjunctive accents (munach, merkha), which join a word to the next.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עַל is joined to פְּנֵי by a maqqef: the two are read as one unit, with the stress on פְּנֵי. The same phrase appears again later in the verse. The atnah stands on תְהוֹם, 'the deep', at the end of the first half; the second half ends with הַמָּיִם and the sof pasuq.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A short verse with two halves. יְהִי, 'let there be', carries a conjunctive accent, munach, and joins אוֹר, 'light', which carries the atnah and ends the first half. The second half, 'and there was light', ends with the same word אוֹר, now carrying the silluq and the sof pasuq. In the second half, וַיְהִי is joined to אוֹר by a maqqef.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two maqqefs. אֶת is joined to הָאוֹר, 'the light', and כִּי, 'that', is joined to טוֹב, 'good'; each pair is read as one unit. The atnah is on טוֹב, so 'And God saw the light, that it was good' is the first half. The second half is 'and God divided the light from the darkness'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יוֹם carries a zaqef, a smaller division inside the first half of the verse. לָיְלָה carries the atnah, which ends the first half. אֶחָד carries the silluq and the sof pasuq. The verse thus has two parts and the first part has two sub-parts: God named the light 'day', and the darkness he named 'night'.
